## TL;DR

This QA pass found that the task UI could not set prerequisites during create or edit, and that long candidate titles could widen the prerequisite list. I added a searchable picker, wired it to the existing create and update API fields, constrained its layout, and added interaction and rendered-layout coverage. The auth-less server remained read-only; headless browser requests exercised the UI through intercepted successful responses, while existing backend tests covered persistence and validation. The final review captures report both states without blocking console errors.

## Work and rationale

I began with the task’s required hands-on check of creation, editing, screenshot attachment, and dependencies at desktop and phone widths. The initial review found that the QA note did not establish the requested behaviors. I traced the failed Create interaction to the read-only preview guard: `just serve-noauth` starts the preview child, which correctly rejects writes. I did not weaken or bypass that guard.

The server already accepted `dependsOn` on task creation and PATCH, and it validated unknown IDs, self-dependencies, and cycles. The UI did not offer a way to set dependencies. I added `TaskDependencyPicker.vue` with title and ID search, current-task exclusion, bounded results, multi-select, and removal. Manual task creation and the task Details editor both use it; the form sends dependency IDs through the existing API fields. The store initializes and resets the creation field so selections do not leak into later tasks. Tests cover filtering, exclusion, selection, removal, and create/update request bodies.

I drove the UI in headless Playwright against the auth-less preview at 1280 and 375 pixels. GET requests used the server; Playwright intercepted only successful POST/PATCH requests because the server is read-only. The creation flow selected a prerequisite and screenshot, checked the request bodies, and observed the success transition. The Details flow selected a prerequisite, checked its PATCH body, and observed the saved state. This verifies UI payloads and success handling, not browser-session persistence. Existing backend tests exercise task creation, attachment storage, dependency serialization, persistence, and graph validation. The QA note records this evidence boundary.

The rendered contrast audit later found that the picker’s small status text fell below the contrast floor in Solarized Dark. I changed status, empty-state, and selected-dependency copy to use the foreground token. A subsequent review capture revealed a long candidate title widening the options list. I constrained the list, rows, and buttons to the picker width; the title flexes into the remaining space and truncates. A headless WebKit regression test checks the real rendered geometry with long labels at 375 and 1280 pixels, including that the list and buttons have no horizontal overflow.

## Approaches tried

I first followed the required auth-less preview setup and inspected the rejected create request. The router’s preview guard explained the rejection. I considered a writable `repoos serve --preview-overrides` instance, but the managed-agent CLI rejected launching a direct server; I kept the supported read-only setup and intercepted only the UI writes. This paired honest UI evidence with existing persistence tests. For the overflow bug, I added a WebKit layout assertion rather than a source-only CSS check, because a DOM-only test cannot measure flex sizing and scroll width.

## Challenges and blockers

The preview server cannot perform writes by design, and a direct writable server was unavailable in this managed session. Therefore this browser pass does not independently establish persisted task creation, screenshot storage, or dependency updates. The existing API and core tests cover those paths. Handoff screenshots are generated from the declared create and edit states. I did not edit `repoos.toml`.

## Key learnings

The backend dependency contract existed before the UI supported it; tracing the full user path exposed that gap. Preview write failures are expected, so browser requests must be described as mocked when the server intentionally rejects mutations. For layout bugs, generated captures can reveal flex sizing failures that component tests miss; a small real-browser geometry test protects against regression. The audit also showed that small status text needs the theme foreground token to stay readable across all supported palettes.
